articles.title: Trump tells 60 Minutes undocumented workers like landscapers and hotel maids could be allowed to stay in bipartisan deal
articles.summary: The president made the comment the same day he promoted Stephen Miller — a hard-liner in favor of sharply restricting immigration — as the White House chief...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has suggested that undocumented landscapers, hotel maids, restaurant employees and others could be allowed to stay in a bipartisan immigration deal negotiated with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

"Well, the deal would be we would work something out," Trump told "60 Minutes" on CBS News in an interview that was taped on Nov. 6 and aired Nov. 8. "And I think it's something-- I think that's something that's actually doable."

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

"When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's worked there as — you know, as a maid, as a cleaner…great jobs, and all of a sudden, they're being taken outta the country, it's tough," Trump said. "It's a tough thing."

Trump's remarks were made on the same day he promoted Stephen Miller , a hard-liner in favor of sharply restricting immigration, to the White House chief of staff post. Democratic leaders quickly bashed the promotion , with one calling for Miller to be fired.

The president, though, has issued mixed signals on immigration since the interview aired. He later affirmed his support for an immigration policy that doesn't confer legal status on people residing in the U.S. without authorization. "We have a very strong deportation policy. There's no amnesty," he said at a Nov. 9 press conference . "We keep that, but we focus on the worst of the worst."

In the "60 Minutes" interview, Trump credited his hard-line immigration policy for bolstering support, but admitted it also dissuaded some voters from backing the Republicans in the midterms.

"I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," he said. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

He also cracked the door open to a deal for unauthorized immigrants, particularly for those who have been paying federal income and payroll taxes, as a large share already do.

"There's a large part of the country that think they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel or doing something," Trump said. "And in some cases, paying taxes."

articles.title: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
articles.summary: After a New York Times report that Jensen Huang had an affair with another Nvidia executive, now there’s a rumor the board will fire him.
articles.body: Nvidia’s board is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang following a report from the New York Times about a second alleged extramarital affair, just days after he admitted to a separate affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reports. The second alleged affair was with an executive who reports to him, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to the Times. The Nvidia board will meet as soon as today to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge. Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times. The Times has not seen the video. Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background. Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday. Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to handle it, but today’s rumor suggests it won’t wait for those results to act. Last year, Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller known for handling public sex scandals, according to Wired. Its founder has advised several powerful men who faced public scrutiny, Wired reported, like former congressman Anthony Weiner and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.

articles.title: Trump Plans to Sell Public Land, Reducing Size of Federal Estate
articles.summary: The Trump administration has formally said it plans to sell public lands as part of a plan to reduce the size of the federal estate.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The Trump administration has formally said it plans to sell public lands as part of a plan to reduce the size of the federal estate.

The Interior Department's four-year strategic plan released on Wednesday didn't specify how much land it plans to sell or how the land would be priced. The department, which manages some 480 million acres, didn't immediately respond to a request for more details.

"The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands," the agency said in the document. "Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands."

The Interior Department alongside the Department of Housing and Urban Development has previously called for building housing on "underutilized" federal land. But the inclusion of the land sales marks the first time the agency has officially confirmed it wants to sell federal land, said Jayson O'Neill, a spokesman for Save Our Parks, a watchdog group. He pointed out Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has previously said selling public land wasn't part of the Trump administration's agenda.

"Doug Burgum just said the quiet part out loud, confirming that the Trump administration will work to sell off America's shared public lands," O'Neill said in an email.

Burgum, a former technology executive who served as North Dakota's governor, has often talked about viewing the nation's vast federal lands, and the oil, gas, and minerals contained within, as part of "America's balance sheet," worth trillions of dollars.

Congressional condemnation of the plan was swift. Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, who is poised to lead the Senate energy committee next year, said he would oppose efforts to sell or privatize public lands.

"These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in," Heinrich said in a statement. "Public lands belong in public hands."
